subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (3, −3, 4), (2, −3, 4) and (0, −1, 1), then show that A⁻¹ = A³.

mark_split.label: Restate the claim as A⁴ = I

recall_prompt: Say how you would show that the inverse of A equals A cubed — say what you would prove instead.

steps.label: Restate as A⁴ = I
steps.margin_note: First mark, and the idea of the question. Multiply both sides by A: A⁻¹ = A³ becomes AA⁻¹ = AA³, that is I = A⁴. Finding A⁴ is arithmetic; finding A⁻¹ would be nine cofactors.
lines: A⁻¹ = A³  ⇔  AA⁻¹ = AA³  ⇔  I = A⁴
So it is enough to show A⁴ = I.

recall.must_convey: That the claim is restated by multiplying both sides by A, turning A⁻¹ = A³ into A⁴ = I, which avoids computing an inverse at all.
accept: multiply both sides by A so A inverse equals A cubed becomes A to the fourth equals I
restate it as A power four equals the identity, then no inverse is needed
instead of finding the inverse show A to the four is I
rendu vaipula A tho multiply cheste A power four equals I avthundi
it is enough to prove A to the fourth equals the identity matrix

steps.why: A⁻¹ is defined by AA⁻¹ = I, so any statement about A⁻¹ can be turned into one about products of A. That swap is what makes this a 4-mark question instead of a 7-mark one.
common_mistakes: Computing A⁻¹ by cofactors and running out of time.
Multiplying only one side by A.

steps.label: Find A²
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Nine row-by-column products. The middle row of A has a 0 in it, which shortens three of them — but every entry still has to be written out.

recall.must_convey: That A² is found by multiplying A by itself row against column, giving rows (3,−4,4), (0,−1,0), (−2,2,−3).
accept: multiply A by itself row into column to get A squared
A squared is A times A, not the entries squared
work out the nine products to get A squared
A ni A tho multiply cheste A square vasthundi, row into column
find A into A carefully with the negative entries

steps.why: A⁴ is (A²)², so computing A² once and squaring it costs two multiplications instead of three. Reaching for A³ first would be a wasted step here.
common_mistakes: Squaring each entry instead of multiplying the matrices.
Sign slips where two negatives meet.
Computing A³ instead, which does not square as cleanly.

steps.label: Show A⁴ = I
steps.margin_note: Last mark. A⁴ = (A²)(A²) — square the matrix just found. It comes out as the identity, which is exactly what was required.
lines: Since A⁴ = I, multiplying by A⁻¹ gives A³ = A⁻¹.

recall.must_convey: That A⁴ is found as A² times A², comes out as the identity, and that A⁴ = I is what proves A⁻¹ = A³.
accept: A to the fourth is A squared times A squared and it comes out as the identity so A inverse equals A cubed
square A squared to get I which proves the result
A four equals I hence A inverse is A cubed
A square ni A square tho multiply cheste I vasthundi, so A inverse equals A cube
the product is the identity matrix so the claim holds

steps.why: A matrix whose fourth power is the identity is its own inverse three steps along. Writing the final line back in terms of A⁻¹ is what answers the question actually asked.
common_mistakes: Reaching A⁴ = I and stopping, without returning to A⁻¹ = A³.
